overview: Antarctica is a continent whose modern human communities center on expedition and research stations. It has no Indigenous resident population. Scientific cooperation operates alongside differing national positions on territorial claims. Its human history includes practical engineering, shared living, environmental discoveries and agreements about how people should work there.

periods.title: An expedition base at Cape Evans
periods.summary: Scott’s expedition built its hut in January 1911. Later used by Shackleton’s Ross Sea party, the base preserves evidence of science, transport and provisioning before the survivors were rescued in 1917.

periods.title: Cooperation leads to a treaty
periods.summary: Countries active in the International Geophysical Year of 1957 and 1958 negotiated an Antarctic Treaty, signed in December 1959. It entered into force in 1961.

periods.title: Changing access to fieldwork
periods.summary: Janet Thomson worked inside the Antarctic Circle as a BAS scientist in 1983. Women’s access to fieldwork and winter stations expanded unevenly across programs.

periods.title: The ozone hole is reported
periods.summary: Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin published evidence of severe springtime ozone loss above Antarctica. The discovery helped prompt international action against ozone-depleting chemicals.

periods.title: Environmental protection becomes a treaty commitment
periods.summary: The Environmental Protocol was signed in Madrid in 1991 and entered into force in 1998. It prohibited mineral-resource activities except scientific research and strengthened environmental protection.

periods.title: Everyday engineering at research stations
periods.summary: Australian program descriptions show how stored food, hydroponic vegetables, treated water and conservation practices support people through winter isolation.

periods.title: Snowmelt exposes expedition remains
periods.summary: Conservators documented previously hidden or rarely visible objects around Cape Evans, including stored mutton, equipment and remains associated with dog care.

periods.title: A more precise climate chronology
periods.summary: Researchers revised the dating of the EPICA Dome C ice core, improving the comparison of Antarctic climate records with other environmental archives.

items.text: The Cape Evans hut was prefabricated in London and assembled in Antarctica in January 1911. Its floor, walls and roof used insulating layers including finely shredded seaweed. Stables stood beside the main building. The surviving structure shows how imported construction materials, animal transport and indoor working space were combined to support an expedition.

In 2022, reduced snow cover exposed mutton carcasses wrapped in muslin near Cape Evans. The conservation team linked them to meat brought from New Zealand by either Scott’s expedition or Shackleton’s Ross Sea party and stored in a snow cave. The find records cold storage and overseas provisioning, while its exact expedition attribution remains uncertain.

The same season exposed small stretcher-like remains made from packing cases and bamboo in the area called the dog hospital. Conservator Al Fastier interpreted them as equipment for moving injured dogs. A hardwood bench used for gravity measurements also became fully visible. Together, these objects illuminate animal care and scientific work beyond the hut’s living quarters.

Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin reported the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985. Long-running measurements revealed severe seasonal loss in the protective ozone layer. A Dobson spectrophotometer at Halley is a concrete example of the instrumentation behind this research. The discovery connected observations at a remote station with a global atmospheric problem.

The discovery helped drive the international response that produced the Montreal Protocol in 1987. The connection matters because Antarctic research could identify harm caused by chemicals used far from the continent. The ozone hole is a thinning of atmospheric ozone, not a hole in the ice or the same phenomenon as global warming.

The EPICA Dome C drilling reached 3,260 meters into East Antarctic ice. Its record spans about 800,000 years, allowing scientists to investigate repeated climate changes. Measurements from ancient ice and trapped air must be placed on a dated sequence before researchers can compare their timing with records elsewhere.

Bouchet and colleagues’ 2023 chronology combined new measurements, age markers and models. They reported that average dating uncertainty across the long record fell from about 1,700 to 900 years. This is an improvement in the timescale, not a claim that every layer has an exact calendar date or that all uncertainty has vanished.

sections.title: Daily life and who gets to participate

items.text: The Australian program’s 2020 account describes chefs preparing shared meals from summer supplies. Much of the food is frozen or tinned to last through winter; hydroponic lettuces and tomatoes supplement stored provisions. The kitchen and growing facilities are part of the infrastructure that makes sustained scientific work possible, while communal dinners also shape social life.

Water cannot simply be taken for granted because the landscape is covered in ice. The program described Casey and Mawson pumping from melt lakes into heated storage, while Davis treated local water through reverse osmosis. Water-saving appliances, shorter showers and careful laundry routines connect engineering systems with daily habits.

Women were excluded from many Antarctic field opportunities even while contributing to research institutions. BAS records Janet Thomson working inside the Antarctic Circle in 1983 and women overwintering at Signy in 1993 and Rothera in 1997. These dates describe changes within one program; participation developed differently in other countries’ expeditions.

Station populations expand during the summer, when travel and fieldwork are easier, and contract in winter. The Australian program identifies McMurdo on Ross Island as the continent’s largest center. Research communities therefore depend on recurring rotations and external transport, rather than forming a single Antarctic nation with a common government.

The Antarctic Treaty protects scientific cooperation and provides for the exchange of observations and inspection of stations. It preserves parties’ differing positions on territorial claims while barring new claims or expansion of existing ones during its operation. Agreement on peaceful research did not require every country to accept another country’s sovereignty claim.

The Environmental Protocol treats Antarctica as a reserve for peace and science and prohibits mineral-resource activities other than research. It has no automatic expiry in 2048: that date concerns a possible review procedure. Environmental protection therefore continues under a legal framework, rather than ending on a predetermined opening day for mining.

ending.text: Antarctica has no single civilization or state whose fall can be dated. Expedition bases have closed or changed use, while research communities and international governance continue. Neither the Antarctic Treaty nor its Environmental Protocol has a termination date. The map’s 1994 endpoint does not mark the end of human activity on the continent.
